title: Indices, Logarithm and Surds Quiz 3
description: The six surd rules, in a gentle first set. Mind the roots of sums.
instructions: Indices, Logarithm and Surds: Simplifying surds.
Write maths answers with the keypad. Any equal form is accepted.
Every question has a trap. Slow down at the signs.

questions.question: Simplify $\sqrt{18}$.
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{9\times2}=\sqrt9\times\sqrt2=3\sqrt2$. Watch out: take the square root of the perfect square: $\sqrt9=3$, not $9$.

questions.question: Simplify $2\sqrt{2}\times3\sqrt{5}$.
questions.explanation: Multiply the numbers outside and the numbers inside: $2\cdot3\cdot\sqrt{2\cdot5}=6\sqrt{10}$. Watch out: you cannot add $2+3$; this is a product.

questions.question: $\sqrt{28}=k\sqrt7$. Find $k$.
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{28}=\sqrt{4\times7}=2\sqrt7$, so $k=2$. Watch out: $28=4\times7$ uses the perfect square $4$, not $14\times2$.

questions.question: Find the value of $(\sqrt{10}+\sqrt{3})(\sqrt{10}-\sqrt{3})$.
questions.explanation: Difference of two squares: $10-3=7$. Watch out: the cross terms cancel, so it is a difference ($10-3$), not a sum.

questions.question: Simplify $5\sqrt{6}+4\sqrt{6}$.
questions.explanation: Like surds add like terms: $(5+4)\sqrt6=9\sqrt6$. Watch out: only the coefficients are added; the root stays $\sqrt6$.

questions.question: $\sqrt{\dfrac{12}{121}}=k\sqrt3$. Give $k$ as a decimal to 3 decimal places.
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{\dfrac{12}{121}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{12}}{\sqrt{121}}=\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{11}$, so $k=\dfrac{2}{11}\approx0.182$. Watch out: split into two roots first, and simplify $\sqrt{12}$ too.

questions.question: Put the steps for simplifying $\sqrt{18}$ in order.
questions.explanation: Find a perfect-square factor, split the root, evaluate the root of the square, then write the result. Watch out: split only after you have found the perfect square.

questions.question: Which of these are **surds**?
questions.explanation: $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt7$ and $\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt3$ are irrational, so they are surds. $\sqrt{16}=4$ and $\sqrt{9/4}=\frac32$ are rational. Watch out: $\sqrt{12}$ can be simplified, but it is still a surd.

questions.question: Simplify $\sqrt{50}+\sqrt{8}$. One step is wrong. Tap it.
questions.explanation: $7\sqrt2$ cannot be turned into $\sqrt{14}$: $7\sqrt2=\sqrt{98}$. Watch out: adding coefficients keeps the root $\sqrt2$.
